newsitem.title: USA: "Old Ironsides" fit for sail of the century.
newsitem.headline: "Old Ironsides" fit for sail of the century.

text.p: The USS Constitution was victorious in 19th century sea battles over British warships, earning its famous nickname "Old Ironsides." Now it has won its war with more recent enemies: age, dry rot and disrepair.
After a $12 million, four-year restoration, the world's oldest commissioned warship still afloat, the Constitution is scheduled on Monday to set sail on its own for the first time in 116 years.
The possibility the 200 year-old American frigate would ever sail again was something few people thought about until recently, Charlie Deans, the warship's chief restorer, said.
"It was always in the back of people's minds. But I believe that it was like, that's a dream that is never going to happen," Deans said.

In the years since the Constitution's battles against the British in the War of 1812, it barely managed to escape the scrapyard. A poem by the American author Oliver Wendell Holmes aroused national support for a restoration in the 1830s, while more than $150,000 in pennies collected by schoolchildren funded another refit between 1927 and 1931.

By 1992, when the Constitution went into the drydock at the Boston Navy Yard for another restoration, most of the masts, the upper deck and other areas above the waterline were rotted and had to be replaced.
About 15 percent of the ship, most of it below the waterline, including the keel and parts of the stern, are original, Deans said.
Live oak, a dense, rot-resistant wood grown only in the southeast United States and Cuba, gave the hull its "iron" strength which repelled cannon fire and helped preserve it to this day.

However, the immense weight of the Constitution's 44 cannons, each between 4,000 pounds (8,800 kg) and 6,000 pounds (13,200 kg), caused the ship to sag, or "hog", at each end of the hull and the keel to bow about 14-1/2 inches in the middle.
"The heart and soul of the ship is the keel, the backbone of the vessel," said Margarita Desy, the associate curator of the USS Constitution Museum in Boston. "Eventually, a hog could snap the keel."
Deans and his crew straightened the keel by resting the ship on a specially-built layer of sand blocks, which were slowly drained until the hull straightened.

But keeping the keel from hogging after a relaunch was another problem. After some detective work consulting old documents and letters, restorers discovered that a series of interlocking beams had originally supported the hull but had been removed during a previous restoration.
Said Robert Gillen, the vessel's former captain: "The ship is wonderfully strong. The way it is now, it can sail in perpetuity, literally."
